Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

text:
PACKET-20 — UNVERIFIED IMAGE READING (blind; no outside source consulted)

Exposure note: nothing in my context proposed an identification or an earlier reading of this fragment.
Several short passages on the page are scriptural quotations that the letters themselves make recognisable
(e.g. "faciam(us) ho(m)i(n)em ad ymagi/ne(m) (et) si(mi)litu(d)i(n)e(m) n(ost)ram ... maris (et) uolatilib(us)
celi"; "ne obliuiscaris / legis mee (et) p(re)cepta ... cor tuu(m)"; "dei factura sum(us) creati in xp̄o
ih(es)u"). Familiarity with that wording may have helped me resolve abraded words INSIDE those quotations;
I have not used it to supply text I cannot see, and I made no attempt to identify the work or author.

=====================================================================
1. LAYOUT SURVEY (image only)
=====================================================================
Observations
- A small parchment fragment (c. 10 cm wide by c. 12.5 cm high by the ruler), labelled "A" on a paper slip,
  photographed on both sides: image-001 (side 1) and image-010 (side 2). Text upright on both.
- Two columns per side, c. 40-42 lines per column, very small Gothic book hand with heavy abbreviation.
- Side 1: left column has lost the first 1-3 letters of most lines at the left edge (small tears/notches
  at that edge); right column is complete in width but its lower two thirds are darkened and abraded.
- Side 2: left column is darkened/abraded over most of its height (top 6 lines under a stain, lower half
  nearly gone); right column is the best-preserved area of the fragment, but a vertical crease/trim line
  near the right edge obscures the last 2-4 letters of most lines, with a notch at c. line 27.
- Red: paraph marks with a long tail drawn out to the left — side 1 at left col. c. line 19 and c. line 36,
  right col. c. line 6 and c. line 37 (at the line end); side 2 right col. at c. lines 6, 18 (line ends) and
  one faint in the left margin of the left col. c. line 33. On side 1 left col. c. line 36 the red mark
  stands in the margin beside a line that begins a new sentence; just above that line a short phrase is
  written in smaller script (interlinear/inter-paragraph addition). Thin dark underlining under a few words
  in side 2 right col. (c. line 20) and in side 1 right col. (c. lines 5 and 8). No running title visible.
Tentative interpretation (not observation)
- Continuous prose that quotes a short phrase, then expounds it in numbered steps ("s(e)c(und)o",
  "t(er)c(i)o") with strings of short proof-citations introduced by a recurring siglum I read as "io." /
  "iō" followed by "d(icit)" or a book reference. The phrase beginning "[..]bliuios(us) fact(us) s(ed)
  f(a)c(t)or op(er)is" (side 1) and the words "auditor no(n) obliuios(us) fact(us)" and "D(icit) g° no(n)
  auditor..." (side 2) suggest one and the same lemma is being worked through on both sides.
- Which side is recto is not established.

=====================================================================
2. SPANS SELECTED / NOT READ
=====================================================================
Selected: side 2 right column (whole, best preserved); side 2 left column lines c. 7-20; side 1 right column
top 11 lines; side 1 left column, the paragraph opening at the lower red mark and a few lines near the top.
Not read: side 1 right column from c. line 12 down (darkened); side 1 left column c. lines 9-34 (only stray
words); side 2 left column lines 1-6 and c. 21-41.
Note on the crops: on side 2 the detail images begin at about line 7 of each column — the top six lines of
both columns appear only in the reduced overview image-010. Likewise image-017 and image-018 show only the
bottom edge and the ruler (no additional text). A detail crop of the top of side 2 would be needed.
The resolution of the detail crops (c. 760-890 px for the whole 10 cm fragment width) is low for this
script size; a higher-resolution image would change many readings below.

Conventions: (..) = proposed expansion; word? = uncertain; [illegible]; [..] = lost at a physical edge or
crease, not supplied. "g°" = the scribe's sign for "ergo". Line numbers are counted from the top of the
named image for the named column, including a partial top line; they may be off by one.
